chapter_theme: Pattinathar's second Koyil Thiruvagaval, one unit. The poet, whose love and thought run after women and who has not won the fortune of wearing the Lord's feet, names his own body in some forty figures: a wilderness raided by the five thieves, a chest of urine and excrement, a casket of the two deeds, a village where wind, bile and phlegm lodge, a stinking pot, a top spinning on the rope of desire, a ship of unending disease, a cage of death, a bellows for rice, a kite in the wind, a log the god of fate cuts, a shirt the four-faced tailor sews, a feast for the pyre, a leaf shrivelled in the fire of lust, a lump that walks as a bridegroom and lies as a corpse, and then a run of the stock images of impermanence, frost before the sun, a rainbow, a cloud's shadow, a bubble, writing on water, a dream, and worse than all these a stain of maya. It ends 'enough, enough, Lord', and asks to be taken and ruled by the dance of bliss while Uma cries 'live'.
structure_note: A confession (lines 1 to 6), the body catalogue in short two-foot phrases (ஆசைக் கயிற்றிலாடும் பம்பரம் and the rest), and a closing petition. The catalogue moves from containers and places (பேழை, பெட்டகம், சீறூர், பாண்டம்) to things driven or cut (பம்பரம், மரக்கலம், கட்டை, சட்டை) to the brief things (பனிக்கூட்டம், இந்திரசாபம், குமிழி, நீர்மேல் எழுத்து, கனவு). The third agaval reuses many of the same phrases.

301.reading: The poet, whose love and thought go only to the quarrelsome, sinful women whose eyes run to their ears and who play with the sore at their hips, and who has not been granted the fortune of wearing the Lord's two lotus feet, describes his own body as a wilderness where the five thieves raid, a chest of urine and excrement, a casket of the two deeds, a hamlet where wind, bile and phlegm lodge, a bloody frame of filthy skin, a stinking pot, a torn rag of four cubits and nine, a garden of bitter gourd, a mound in the great cremation ground, a top spinning on the rope of desire, a ship of ceaseless disease, a changing illusion, a cage of death, a bellows for rice, a kite flying in the wind, a log that fate's Dharma cuts, a shirt the four-faced tailor stitches, a feast thrown to the pyre, a dry leaf shrivelling in the fire of lust, a tuber worms dig, a forked branch up which the shoot of sin climbs, a lump that walks as a bridegroom and ends lying as a corpse, a burden the town will not let lie, a heap of pulai flowers against the wind, frost before the morning sun, a rainbow moving in the sky, the passing shadow of a thundering cloud, a bubble on water, writing on water, a sight seen in sleep's dream, and, worse than all of these, a stain of maya; and says enough, enough, Lord, enough: show the dance of bliss while the daughter of the mountain cries 'live', take me and rule me, for that is the beauty of your grace.
301.nuance: The names fall into kinds: the body as a container of waste, as a thing moved by what is not itself (the top on the rope of desire, the kite in the wind, the puppet of 240), as a thing already prepared for death (the log Dharma cuts, the shirt Brahma sews, the feast for the fire), and as the stock brief things, which the poet caps by saying the body is worse than a bubble or a dream because it is a மாயக் களங்கம், a stain made of maya. சதுர்முகப் பாணன், the four-faced tailor, is Brahma stitching the body; விதிவழித் தருமன் is Yama as Dharma. நான்முழத் தொன்பது பீற்றத் துண்டம் is obscure: a torn cloth four cubits long with nine (holes), or nine torn pieces of four cubits. ஊரிற் கிடக்க ஒட்டா உபாதி uses the Siddhanta word உபாதி loosely for the corpse the town hurries out. The petition at the end is brief, and the grace asked for is to be ruled (ஆண்டுகொண்டருள்), not to be released.

links.note: The Naladiyar's firm-minded see the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts; Pattinathar's catalogue includes the bubble on water (நீரிற் குமிழி) and then says the body is worse, a stain of maya. The Naladiyar makes the image the mark of understanding; Pattinathar treats it as too kind.

Tirumular says the wealth that seemed lasting is like writing on water and tells one to conquer the senses; Pattinathar applies நீர்மேல் எழுத்து to the body itself, among the frost, the rainbow and the dream. The same image moves from possessions to the possessor.

Arunagirinathar names his body as a string of bags, of deceit, of flesh, of anger's toddy, of wind, of rubbish, of pus, and a carcass for dogs; Pattinathar's string runs through chest, casket, hamlet, pot, top, ship, cage, bellows, log, shirt and corpse. Both are catalogues of the body in short phrases ending in a plea; Pattinathar's adds the brief things and the maya stain.

source_issues: Line 12 நான்முழத் தொன்பது பீற்றத் துண்டம் and line 18 தூற்றம் பத்தம் cannot be construed with confidence; the second may be corrupt (தூற்றும் பத்தம், a scattering sheaf, or தூறும் பத்தம்).
Line 29 பிணமாய்க் கிடக்கும் பிண்டம், பிணமேல் runs the next phrase onto the line; the division is the source's.
